newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Bundesbanker threatens Bonn with court over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Bundesbanker threatens Bonn with court over EMU.

text.p: Former Bundesbank council member Wilhelm Noelling confirmed in a press interview published on Sunday his intention to take the federal government to Germany's Constitutional Court if Bonn went ahead with European monetary union while missing strict entry criteria.

Noelling, who retired from the German central bank in 1992, told the weekly newspaper Welt am Sonntag that he believed it would be contrary to the German constitution for Bonn to push ahead with entry into the planned single European currency under such circumstances.

"I and others are determined to go to the Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe if, having clearly missed the entry criteria, the government and the lower and upper houses of parliament agree in spring 1998 to take part," he said.
"I am inviting all German citizens to support this move and to show that we are not a country of sheep," he said in the interview.
Noelling, who currently teaches at the University of Hamburg, made a similar threat last May in a move that received significant attention among German financial market operators.

Economists widely believe that, with unemployment becoming ever more of a burden on state finances, Germany could struggle by the end of this year to meet an EMU requirement that public deficit fall to three percent of gross domestic product.
A European Union summit is scheduled for spring in 1998 to determine which countries will be eligible to join the single currency -- the Euro -- on time in 1999.

While the Maastricht Treaty on the single currency does allow a degree of flexibility in meeting the requirements, the German government has so far insisted that it sees the criteria as not open to loose interpretation. --Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
